title: Defanging Laws and Bringing Home Billions: How Trump Has Rewritten the Corruption Rulebook At Home and Abroad
content:
During his first term in office, U.S. President Donald J. Trump drew criticism for profiting from events held at Trump-branded golf courses and housing foreign delegations at his pricey Washington hotel. 

But upon his return, he has blown past all precedents on personal enrichment while also overseeing the systematic unraveling of American anti-corruption laws, institutions, and norms. 

While many of these moves have been enforced by the U.S. government’s executive branch, the Republican-led Congress has done little to stop the slide — and, in some cases, has even encouraged it.

So when U.S. voters head to the polls on November 3 for midterm elections, it is not just control of the House of Representatives and the Senate that is at stake, but the future of efforts to contain corruption at home and abroad. 

On the eve of the election, OCCRP spoke to experts to take stock of the state of U.S. corruption — and the fight against it —  today, whether Democrats have a plan to reverse course, and what the repercussions of Trump’s actions have been at home and abroad. 

The White House did not respond to requests to comment in time for publication.

title: Five Questions About Trump’s ‘America First’ Approach to Fighting Corruption
content:
Shortly after taking office in early 2025, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump paused the enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the nearly 50-year-old law that prohibits American citizens or companies from bribing foreign officials for business.

When the FCPA was resumed six months later, the U.S. Department of Justice was ordered to narrow its focus to limit “undue burdens” on American companies operating outside the country. That action was in line with the Trump administration’s “America First” unilateral approach to foreign policy, which has seen the U.S. withdraw from dozens of international organizations on the grounds that they are inefficient and not in line with the country’s priorities. 

Lorenzo Crippa, a lecturer at the University of Strathclyde who quantitatively studies how recorded instances of corruption affect financial flows, discusses the repercussions of these changes and worrying trends that have emerged under the new U.S. approach to global anti-corruption enforcement.

title: How IRL Story Lab is Reimagining What Journalism Can Do
content:
The team at the Investigative Reporting Lab (IRL) in North Macedonia carried a frustration familiar to many newsrooms: They would spend months, sometimes a year, unraveling a complex system of corruption and then ask readers to sit through thousands of words to understand it. The information mattered, but the format didn't always do it justice. So they decided to try a new approach.

“We started experimenting with documentary, video, and social storytelling, and we saw very clearly that when you change the way you tell a story, you also change who is willing to engage with it,” says IRL editor in chief Saska Cvetkovska.

That experimentation has now taken IRL somewhere few investigative newsrooms have gone: narrative fiction. Through IRL Story Lab, a production company built inside the newsroom, the team is adapting reporting into film — starting with “The Bench,” a dark comedy inspired by characters in “Spooks and Spin,” a 2017 investigation by IRL and OCCRP into information warfare in the Balkans.

title: ‘Is This Real?’: A Serbian Investigative Journalist Reflects on the Country’s Stunning Election
content:
Sunday’s election marked a turning point in Serbia, with the ruling SNS party of Aleksandar Vučić handed a resounding defeat by a student movement that capitalized on mounting public anger over years of corruption and criminality.

Many of those abuses had been exposed by KRIK, an award-winning Serbian investigative outlet and OCCRP partner that has spent years covering the country’s criminals, its corrupt officials, and the connections between them. In return, its young journalists have withstood pressure most people can scarcely imagine: personal attacks by pro-government tabloids, an endless stream of lawsuits, and even death threats.

Now, a new era is dawning. The seemingly unbreakable control exercised by Vučić — who served as information minister under dictator Slobodan Milošević — has been broken.

In this interview, KRIK editor-in-chief Stevan Dojčinović reflects on what the last few days have meant for him, how the students did it, and what challenges lie ahead. As he spoke with OCCRP late at night, the sounds of celebration filtered in from the street.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: Cambodia Cracked Down on Banks Allegedly Linked to Cyber-Scams. The IMF Says the Problem Persists.
content:
Amid mounting international pressure to clean up its financial system, Cambodia’s central bank published a statement earlier this month accusing unnamed actors of waging a campaign of “economic sabotage” against the country.

“Rumors and unverified information have been circulating on social media, claiming that a number of banking and financial institutions are facing issues or heading toward collapse in the near future,” the National Bank of Cambodia (NBC) said.

The NBC did not clarify who might be behind such a campaign, or which institutions were targeted. But the regulator warned that such “baseless” information could undermine “trust in the overall banking system.”

The banking system has taken a beating recently, as international attention turned to Cambodia’s role as a major hub for cyber-scams targeting victims around the world. Proceeds from scams have allegedly flooded into financial institutions.

title: Five Questions About What’s Behind Nigeria’s Romance Scam Industry
content:
In February, OCCRP tracked down a 31-year-old man to his mansion in Nigeria’s capital Abuja. He had allegedly posed as the Crown Prince of Dubai to con a Romanian businesswoman out of more than $2.5 million in a romance scam, according to his victim and two accomplices. 

This is a well-trodden profession in Nigeria, where large numbers of young men, often facing extreme poverty, have taken to swindling lonely victims in wealthier countries to fill their pockets.  

Yet most of the romance scams originating in Nigeria are not particularly complex or lucrative, says journalist Carlos Barragán.

His recently published book, “The Yahoo Boys,” explores what drives the country's teenage fraudsters — whose nickname comes from the Yahoo email addresses used for “Nigerian prince” scams in the early days of the internet — and the repercussions of their scams in Nigeria and abroad.

title: The Maldives Plans to Offer Residency to the World’s Ultra Rich – And Create Islands From Scratch to Do It
content:
Once an isolated haven for scuba divers searching for technicolor marine life, the shallow turquoise waters of the Noonu Atoll in the Maldives are in the midst of a makeover.

A fleet of dumper trucks, excavators, forklifts, and cranes has moved into the habitat for protected parrot fish and nurse sharks to sculpt 25 artificial islands and islets from over six million cubic metres of sand dredged from the seabed. 

Known as Project Ayla, the $790 million private development will host over 70 luxury dwellings and represents the vanguard of a new government strategy to lure the high-net-worth crowd to the debt-saddled nation. 

A view of the main worksite island for Project Ayla in July 2026. CREDIT: Hassan Moosa/Maldives Independent

Yet beyond the plumes of coral-smothering sediment churned up by the dredgers, opposition politicians and transparency advocates are warning of an even murkier threat: the prospect of a new international tax shelter and potential money-laundering hub carved from the ocean floor.

title: Cocaine Boatmen Are Being Blown Up By US Airstrikes, But The Drugs Keep Flowing From Colombia
content:
First, you hear the high-pitched whine of drones overhead. Next comes the boom of explosions.

“And then in the following days, the sea brings in a jerrycan, pieces of a boat, drugs, people too,” says Alberto, a local businessman living on the Colombian peninsula of La Guajira.

This grim sequence of events has become familiar for those based along this arid strip of desert, whose shores are lapped by a part of the Caribbean Sea that has been the site of some 20 deadly U.S. strikes on speedboats over the past year.

The U.S. military campaign against the alleged “narco-terrorists” manning these vessels, known as Operation Southern Spear, has faded from headline news since the first attack was launched over a year ago on September 2. 

Yet it continues to destroy small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific — with at least 235 dead in some 70 strikes so far — in the face of heavy criticism from legal experts and rights groups, who call it an ineffective program of what are essentially extrajudicial murders.

title: OCCRP Briefing: Power Plays in Central Asia: State Capture, Weaponized Anti-Corruption, and the Rules of Doing Business
content:
Strong economic growth and modernization hide a less cheerful reality across Central Asia, where autocratic regimes are still using state power to capture assets and silence dissent.

Kyrgyzstan reports a strong growth of nearly 11% per year. But as OCCRP journalist Eldiyar Arykbaev noted in this briefing, "the devil is in the details.” This growth comes from gold exports and from the country’s role as a trade middleman between China and Russia, which also helps keep the Russian war economy afloat through sanctions evasion. 

“You won’t see that this economic growth had a positive effect on ordinary people,” Arykbaev said. “There is a very thin layer of people who are winning because of this economic growth: people close to the state, in the president’s circles, and in construction projects funded by the state.”

Leila Nazgül Seiitbek, director of Freedom for Eurasia, explained that Kyrgyz business owners are frequently accused of corruption in order to expropriate their assets — a practice known as “kusturizatsiya,” derived from the Kyrgyz word for "vomiting.”
snippet: Strong economic growth and modernization hide a less cheerful reality across Central Asia, where autocratic regimes are still using state power to capture assets and silence dissent.
